nameStory: Pleurotaenium nodosum gets its scientific name from Greek words meaning 'side ribbon' and 'knotty' - describing its elongated, segmented appearance that looks like a decorative ribbon with knots tied along its length. This microscopic green algae doesn't have a widely-used common name, so scientists and nature enthusiasts typically just call it by its genus name, Pleurotaenium.
description: Pleurotaenium nodosum is a single-celled green algae that's invisible to the naked eye, measuring only about 200-400 micrometers long (roughly the width of a few human hairs). Under a microscope, it appears as an elegant, elongated cylinder with distinct constrictions or 'waists' that give it a segmented, beaded appearance. This tiny organism lives in freshwater and is actually quite beautiful when magnified, looking like a delicate glass ornament with a bright green interior. You'll need a microscope to observe this species, as it's part of the hidden microscopic world that exists in every drop of pond water.

idTips.label: Segmented shape
idTips.description: Under magnification, appears as a long cylinder with distinct constrictions creating a beaded or segmented appearance, like a green sausage link

idTips.label: Cell wall texture
idTips.description: Smooth, glass-like cell wall that appears almost translucent under the microscope

idTips.label: Bright green color
idTips.description: Vivid emerald green chloroplasts (food-making structures) distributed throughout the cell interior

idTips.label: Size range
idTips.description: Typically 200-400 micrometers long - about 4 times longer than it is wide

habitat: Found in clean, freshwater environments throughout New England including pristine ponds, slow-moving streams, and bog pools, particularly in areas with slightly acidic water. This species prefers nutrient-poor waters and is often found among other microscopic algae in the surface films of still water bodies. Look for it in undisturbed woodland pools and sphagnum moss habitats where water quality remains high.

seasonality.spring: Most active during spring months when water temperatures begin to warm and daylight increases, making this the best time to find specimens in pond samples.
seasonality.summer: Continues to be present but may be less abundant during hot summer months, especially in shallow waters that warm significantly.
seasonality.fall: Can still be found in autumn samples, particularly in deeper, more stable water bodies that maintain consistent temperatures.
seasonality.winter: Generally dormant or present in very low numbers during winter months when water temperatures drop significantly.

funFact: Despite being a single cell, Pleurotaenium nodosum can live for several weeks and actually 'walks' through the water by secreting mucilage (a slimy substance) from pores in its cell wall - essentially gliding along like a microscopic slug!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other elongated desmid algae like Closterium, but Pleurotaenium's distinctive segmented, beaded appearance with clear constrictions sets it apart from the smooth, crescent-shaped Closterium cells. Memory trick: Pleurotaenium has 'nodes' (bumps) - think 'nodosum' equals 'nodules.'
contextualKnowledge: This organism belongs to a group called desmids, which are considered among the most beautiful microscopic life forms due to their intricate, symmetrical shapes. Many people are surprised to learn that such elegant, almost crystalline structures are actually living, single-celled organisms rather than tiny works of art.
compareHints: Pleurotaenium nodosum differs from its relatives like P. ehrenbergii by having more pronounced constrictions and a more distinctly segmented appearance. While P. trabecula tends to be straighter and more uniform, P. nodosum shows clear 'waisted' sections that create its characteristic beaded look. P. maximum, as its name suggests, is significantly larger and more robust than the relatively slender P. nodosum.
